**My reasoning:**

My family has farmed this land for generations. I know this soil. My land is about 6 mu — my husband handles some of the heavy work but my sons went to the city years ago, so mostly I manage it myself now, and I hire day laborers for harvest. I have no schooling but I've been farming since I was a girl. I know what grows here and what doesn't.

Here in Quzhou, everyone grows wheat and corn. That's what the land is for. Winter wheat goes in after the autumn harvest, comes out in June. Then we turn right around and plant corn in the same field. Two harvests a year. That's how it's always been done here and that's what I'll do.

For wheat seed, I'll buy from the village supply cooperative — the improved variety they've been recommending for a few years now. For corn, I'll buy hybrid seed the same way. Everyone uses hybrid corn now; the yields are clearly better, even I can see that. I won't go back to saving my own corn seed.

For fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer when I plant, then I add urea when the wheat joints and when the corn tassels. I've learned those timing points from watching the crops and from talking to neighbors over the years. I use roughly what I've always used — not more, not less.

Water is a worry. The wells are deeper than when I was young. I'll water the wheat three times: before it goes dormant, at jointing, and at grain fill. Corn needs water at planting if the soil is dry, and again when it silks.

For corn I won't plow — I plant straight into the wheat stubble with the hand-pushed planter my neighbor lends me. For wheat I'll hire the rotary tiller.

I'll spray for aphids on the wheat in spring and check the corn for armyworm in summer. Two sprayings each should be enough in a normal year.
